name: Intercontinental Championship
epitaph: Twenty-eight reigns, headlined by Corporal Punishment's own three separate runs and Lyle Wile's 113-day reign, the longest in the belt's history; Jay Phoenix held it 53 days in 2001, between Celest's two reigns. Jaxx's own second reign is the final Intercontinental Championship the GIWF's own record names. Restarts as the UWF's own Intercontinental Championship.

name: North American Championship
epitaph: Briefly renamed the “Native American Title” during Jay Phoenix's own reign — the fed's own Quick Facts crediting its creation to “Jay Phoenix's overwhelming egoti—*shot*” — and, in an earlier stretch, the belt Lew Spectre vacated by throwing it in a trash can, only for Daneel McCord to retrieve it three days later; also carried, in later use, as the “European Title.” Restarts as the UWF's own North American Championship.

name: North American Tag Team Championship
epitaph: Added September 1999, briefly disbanded after The Dark Lords' own reign and revived by tournament seven months later. The Phenomenons held it three times, the second a 112-day reign, the belt's own longest; Street Science's own win over the Phenomenons and the Bringers of Darkness, 4 July 2001, is the fed's own last recorded change of this title.

name: Regal Rumble
epitaph: An annual over-the-top-rope elimination match, crowning an individual rather than a stable. Two champions are on the surviving record: Blaze on 30 January 2000, and Ricky Ketsu-Eki at the Regal Rumble 2001 PPV, over runner-up Craig Wright.

name: Stable Wars
epitaph: A four-team elimination tournament crowning a stable rather than a single champion, run every May from the fed's own founding year. Three champions are on the surviving record: the Youngbloods in 1999, the Order of the Hammer in 2000, and the Faux-Youngbloods in 2001. The format outlived the fed that invented it — the UWF picked the honor up whole and ran it all the way to a sixth edition.

name: Television Championship
epitaph: The fed's hot-potato belt — 68 changes of hands across the run, more than any other GIWF title. Jay Phoenix held it 13 days in 2000 under the ring name Inferno. Blade's own final reign, the fed's last recorded TV Championship change, closes on a vacancy: he “vacated the title before it was retired.” Restarts as the UWF's own Television Championship.

name: (T)he (H)ardcore (C)hampionship
epitaph: Added January 2000 and, by the fed's own admission, “never officially recognized by the GIWF” — its shortest reign lasted roughly seven minutes (Lew Spectre's tournament win, immediately “defeated” by Ace Thunder), its longest 95 days (Gurgles), and its last GIWF holder, L.U.C.A.B.O.T., “to this day has never been able to rid himself of the title.” Restarts as the UWF's own THC, later salvaged as a physical belt by Gurgles after the UWF's own hardcore title was banned.

name: World Heavyweight Championship
epitaph: Twenty-four reigns across the promotion's own run, opening on Akira's tournament win and closing on Gurgles's second, 89-day reign — the longest of the belt's GIWF life and its final one on record. The lineage restarts as the UWF's own World Heavyweight Championship at the September 2001 tournament that opened the new fed.

name: World Tag Team Championship
epitaph: The Phenomenons' own first tag title — three reigns across the fed's run, the last an 89-day hold — in a lineage that also crowned the Dragoons, the Fomorians (won in what the record calls “the Dublin pub brawl”), and, at the close, Street Science's own 89-day final reign. Restarts as the UWF's own World Tag Team Championship.
